name: Langley, British Columbia
note: Fishing locations for this city. Downloaded with the city's map, not bundled with the app. Every record here is marked unverified: the water, the species, the months and the hazards are researched, and the access scores and depth profiles are deliberately absent because inventing those is what gets somebody stuck in mud with nowhere to park.

spots.name: Derby Reach Regional Park
spots.blurb: Metro Vancouver park on the south bank of the Fraser with a long walkable gravel shoreline, the Edgewater Bar campground and a boat launch. The best-known shore fishery in Langley and the one most people mean when they say they fished the Fraser here.
spots.hazards: This is a big tidal river with a deceptive pull. The gravel shelves off fast, the level moves with the tide as well as the freshet, and the water is cold and silty enough that you will not see the bottom drop away. Wear a belt, not waders you cannot get out of. Freshet from late May through July runs high, fast and full of debris.
spots.tip: Tidal water, so the licence is the DFO Tidal Waters Sport Fishing Licence, not the provincial freshwater one — the boundary is the CPR bridge at Mission, well upstream of here. Fish the last of the flood and the first of the ebb.

spots.name: Fort Langley & Bedford Channel
spots.blurb: The back channel between the village and McMillan Island, quieter and slower than the main river, with the village wharf and the Marina Park shoreline at the top of it. Slack water in a river that mostly has none.
spots.hazards: Tidal channel — it drains to mud flats at low water and the soft ground at the margins will take a boot. Check the tide before walking out onto anything that looks like a bar.
spots.tip: Slack water is why sea-run cutthroat hold here. Small spinners and fry patterns along the island side rather than heavy bottom gear.

spots.name: Glen Valley Regional Park
spots.area: East Langley, on the Abbotsford line
spots.water: Fraser River — Two Bit Bar and Duncan Bar
spots.blurb: Two gravel bars with parking almost on the water, upstream of Fort Langley on the Langley–Abbotsford boundary. Classic lower-Fraser bar fishing: you walk out onto the bar and cast into the seam.
spots.hazards: A gravel bar in a tidal river is the single most dangerous kind of shore fishing here. The bar is walkable at one level and cut off at another, the channel behind it fills, and the drop at the edge is abrupt. Never fish a bar alone and never without knowing the tide and the river level.
spots.tip: Still tidal at this point — the Mission bridge boundary is upstream. Bar fishing works on moving water, so pick the ebb; the seam where the fast water meets the slack off the bar is the whole spot.

spots.name: Salmon River
spots.blurb: A small tributary that runs the length of the township and enters the Fraser at Fort Langley. Sea-run cutthroat push up it, and coho and chum use the lower reaches. Genuinely small water — think a stream you can cast across.
spots.hazards: Almost all of this river runs through private farmland. Bank access is limited to road crossings and the parks, and walking a field to reach it is trespass. Brush and undercut banks throughout.
spots.tip: Non-tidal above the mouth, so this is a provincial freshwater licence — and small Lower Mainland tributaries carry stream-specific closures and non-retention rules protecting wild stocks. Read the synopsis for this stream by name before you fish it.

spots.name: Nicomekl River
spots.water: Nicomekl River — drains to Mud Bay
spots.blurb: The other side of the divide: the Nicomekl runs south and west out of Langley through Surrey to Mud Bay at Blackie Spit, rather than north to the Fraser. Coho, chum, chinook and pink use the watershed, with cutthroat and rainbow above them.
spots.hazards: Slow, low-gradient and soft-banked, with farm and road runoff along much of it — this river has had pollution incidents, including a discharge that killed fish outright. Do not eat anything out of it without checking for a current advisory.
spots.tip: The lower river past the Surrey sea dam is tidal and the upper river is not, so which licence you need depends on where you stand. Work out which side of the dam you are on before you start.

spots.name: Campbell Valley Regional Park
spots.blurb: Large regional park in the south of the township with the Little Campbell running through it. The river is over 30 km long, drains to Semiahmoo Bay, and holds wild coho, chinook, chum, steelhead and cutthroat across its length — but what is inside the park is the small headwater end of it.
spots.hazards: Small headwater stream in a busy park. Much of the streambank is fenced or signed as restored spawning habitat and walking it does real damage. This is a watch-the-fish park more than a catch-the-fish park.
spots.tip: Check the synopsis for closures on the Little Campbell by name first — headwater reaches of Lower Mainland streams are frequently closed outright to protect spawning. If it is closed, Whonnock or Alouette is the honest alternative.

spots.name: Whonnock Lake
spots.blurb: A small municipal lake stocked twice a year by the Freshwater Fisheries Society of BC with catchable rainbow trout in the 200–300 g range, with cutthroat in it as well. Park, beach, and a canoe club on the shore. The easiest fishing in this region and the one to take a child to.
spots.hazards: Shallow, warm and weedy by late summer, which puts the trout off the margins and down. A swimming beach and a paddling club share the water — busy summer weekends are not fishing time here.
spots.tip: Stocked stillwater on a provincial freshwater licence, no tidal complication. Shore fishing works but it is a boat or a float tube lake really; the stocking runs spring and fall, which is also when it fishes.

spots.name: Alouette Lake
spots.blurb: A long reservoir in Golden Ears Provincial Park, stocked in alternate years with cutthroat and rainbow. Day-use area, beach and boat launch at the south end; the rest of it is a deep mountain lake with almost no road access.
spots.hazards: Deep, cold reservoir water and a wind that funnels down the valley in the afternoon — it can be flat at the launch and rough a kilometre up. Drawdown leaves stumps and deadheads near the surface. Park gates close at dusk.
spots.tip: Provincial freshwater licence, and a park day-use fee at the gate. Trolling the drop-offs out from the day-use beach is how this lake is normally fished; from shore, the launch area and the creek mouths are the spots.
